title: Mould remediation
estimatedMinutesNote: Estimated, not verified. Rule: learner text 3503 words / 100 per minute + 3 min per knowledge check (12) + 5 min allowance, rounded to nearest 5, minimum 15.

instruction.heading: Module authority and restricted work
instruction.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to remediate, demolish, disturb building materials, handle contaminated water or waste, or certify that a building, room or occupant area is safe or free of mould or pathogens. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Restricted or high-exposure remediation is carried out only by an appropriately qualified and competent professional under an approved plan, and some related work, including asbestos and lead disturbance and certain waste handling, is restricted to licensed or specially authorised people. The owner, manager, tenant or contract may define what work is permitted, but where the contract covers only routine cleaning, that is the limit of the task. Where the controlling authority or the competent supervisor is not identified, stop and refer.

instruction.heading: 1. Scope, competence and site authority
instruction.body: Before any practical work, confirm the contract boundaries, the responsible remediation manager, the property access permission and the competence of each worker. The lesson is a framework for judgement, not a licence for restricted remediation. A competent supervisor must approve the risk assessment, the worker competence and the protective arrangements. Begin by writing down what has been observed and what is still uncertain. Record who can authorise access, who is accountable for each decision and which conditions require work to stop. If conditions differ from the approved plan, isolate access where that can be done safely and obtain a revised decision before work resumes. The absence of visible growth does not mean there is no hidden damage. In a scenario where a tenant asks a cleaner to treat a damp bedroom after a long leak, while the agreed work order covers only routine cleaning, the cleaner has no authority to treat the room. Establish who may decide, what information is missing and which actions must stop. A generic cleaning certificate cannot replace project-specific remediation competence. In training, build a task-authorisation record that lists permitted inspection only, specialist referral, the occupants, and the destructive work that is excluded.

instruction.heading: 2. Moisture sources and building history
instruction.body: Mould usually follows moisture, so identify the possible sources: roof, plumbing, condensation and the building envelope. Separate what has been observed from what has been assumed. A newly painted wall that smells musty after rain, while the adjacent carpet feels dry, shows that the moisture source may be somewhere other than where it appears, and that the paint may be hiding the problem. Use a non-invasive moisture-history questionnaire and a photograph log, and refer the question of the source to a qualified building investigation. Source correction is necessary to prevent recurrence, because cleaning or repainting a source that is still wet will not stop the growth. In training, draft the questionnaire, the photograph log and the referral note using a fictional property.

instruction.heading: 3. Inspection, concealed damage and escalation
instruction.body: Inspection identifies visible growth and the warning signs of concealed damage without disturbing wall cavities or releasing settled particles. Warning signs include recurring staining, musty odour, bulging or softening surfaces, and cold or wet patches on walls. Do not open cavities or disturb material to look for hidden growth without the approved plan. Where a manager asks for immediate demolition of a sealed cupboard that has recurring staining, the request is not a decision that a cleaner can accept. Demolition needs a revised scope, a competent assessment and specialist investigation, and it must be stopped until those are in place. In training, create a stop-work decision tree and a controlled referral note for concealed damage.

instruction.heading: 4. Occupant health and communication
instruction.body: Plan clear communications with occupants. Protect people who are more sensitive to mould, including those with respiratory conditions, children, older people and people who are unwell. Do not make unsupported medical or safety-clearance statements. When an occupant with respiratory symptoms asks a cleaner whether the room is now safe, the cleaner must not answer with a clearance. Instead, record the scope of the work, state what has and has not been verified, and refer the health question to a clinician. Keep three things apart: observations, medical advice and clearance decisions. In training, role-play a factual communication that records the scope and refers health questions to clinicians.

instruction.heading: 5. Hazard screening and contaminated water
instruction.body: Some hazards lie outside ordinary mould cleaning. Flood or sewage-affected material must be treated as contaminated water, and disturbing old building materials may release asbestos or lead. A ceiling collapse that reveals suspicious old insulation below sewage-affected plasterboard presents both hazards together. Stop work, isolate the area and escalate. Presumed asbestos must not be disturbed by an ordinary cleaner, and any sampling or removal must be carried out by a competent and, where the law requires, licensed person. Contaminated water and unknown building materials demand different controls, and each needs its own assessment. In training, document the isolation and escalation with a simulated risk register.

instruction.heading: 6. PPE, respiratory protection and worker readiness
instruction.body: PPE must match the evaluated exposure and the approved plan. Where respiratory protection is used, the employer's respirator program, the worker's training and the fit requirements must be checked before use. A worker who brings a loose disposable mask and insists it is adequate for major demolition has not met the requirement. Equipment choice does not replace exposure controls, and it cannot be relied on alone. Stop until a competent person has assessed the exposure, selected the equipment and confirmed the worker's readiness. In training, audit a simulated PPE selection and training record, and escalate each deficiency you find.

instruction.heading: 7. Containment and cross-contamination prevention
instruction.body: Containment protects occupants who are not doing the work and keeps clean materials clean. Understand the project-specific containment concepts and the site zoning that the approved plan sets out. Cleaning activity may carry airborne particles into an occupied corridor, so the route must be planned before the work starts. Containment is an approved, supervised measure and is not an unsupervised task for a general cleaner. An experienced remediation manager is needed where the containment is complex or where occupants are close to the work. In training, sketch an approval-only zoning and communication plan, and do not perform containment as a task.

instruction.heading: 8. Porous, semi-porous and hard material decisions
instruction.body: Materials respond differently to moisture and to cleaning. Saturated drywall and timber sitting beside washable metal fixtures need different decisions. Some porous items cannot be reliably cleaned, so demolition or salvage decisions need competent project oversight rather than a cleaning method. Material compatibility decisions are made case by case and are not replaced by a blanket chemical treatment. In training, classify representative mock material cards according to their uncertainty and their likely referral, rather than prescribing how each one should be disposed of.

instruction.heading: 9. Cleaning methods and equipment limits
instruction.body: Cleaning methods for a contaminated area must come from the approved remediation plan. A domestic vacuum and aggressive dry brushing are not suitable for a contaminated area, because they can throw spores and fragments into the air. Aerosol generation and equipment leaks can increase exposure, so equipment must be fitted, maintained and used under the manufacturer's instructions and the plan. HEPA-rated equipment is only as good as its fit, its seals and its maintenance. In training, compare the proposed methods against an approved plan, and identify each unsuitable option and the reason it is unsuitable.

instruction.heading: 10. Waste segregation and environmental handover
instruction.body: Plan the containment of any suspect waste and verify the local disposal, transport and contractor authorisations before the waste is handled. A contractor who suggests putting demolition debris into ordinary office waste bins is proposing something that must be refused. Local waste rules govern, and generic best practice does not replace them. In training, complete a mock waste-routing and authorised-handover worksheet, and identify the two conditions that require specialist referral or supervisor reauthorisation.

instruction.heading: 11. Moisture correction, drying and recurrence prevention
instruction.body: A landlord who wants new paint before a leak is fixed is asking for a result that will not last. Painting over affected surfaces does not remedy dampness, and the mould will return. Map the dependencies between the leak repair, the moisture re-evaluation and the reoccupation decision. Link any proposed cleaning plan to corrected moisture intrusion, follow-up monitoring and documented repairs. In training, create a dependency map for leak repair, moisture re-evaluation and reoccupation decision-making.

instruction.heading: 12. Verification, records and release boundaries
instruction.body: A customer who requests a pathogen-free certificate after visual cleaning is asking for a claim the work does not support. Keep three things apart: task completion, visual review and independent clearance. Only an independent, competent reviewer can clear an area, and the reviewer must be authorised under the applicable requirements. Prepare a factual closeout report that notes the unverified areas and the independent reviewer requirements. Document the observations, the methods used, the changes made, the limitations, and who has authority for post-remediation verification. Reoccupation decisions follow the applicable local and contractual requirements and are separate from task completion.

instruction.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
instruction.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: the hazards are unknown or changing; the work is destructive or hazardous and outside the authorised scope; exposure is uncontrolled or the building is unsafe to occupy; supervision, equipment or permissions are insufficient; flood, sewage, asbestos or lead may be present; a worker's PPE or respirator readiness has not been verified; a client asks for a clearance or pathogen-free statement; or a waste route is unauthorised. A stop-work decision is correct. Record it and restart only after the competent supervisor has confirmed the scope in writing.

procedure: Stop work. Keep occupants and unauthorised people out of the affected area, and isolate access where this can be done safely.
Confirm in writing the scope of the authorised work, the responsible remediation manager and the access permission.
Record the observations, the reported history, the evidence source and any unknown moisture source.
If flood, sewage, asbestos or lead may be present, do not disturb the material. Escalate to a competent and, where required, licensed person.
Confirm the PPE, respirator program, training and fit before any worker enters a contaminated area.
Refer the moisture source to a qualified building investigation, and link any cleaning plan to the corrected source.
Refer occupant health questions to a clinician. Make no medical or clearance statement.
Issue a factual closeout report that separates task completion, visual review and independent clearance, and names the unverified areas.

workedExamples.situation: A tenant asks a cleaner to treat a damp bedroom after a long leak. The agreed work order covers only routine cleaning.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Who may decide, what is missing, and what must stop?
workedExamples.reasoning: The cleaner cannot decide. The work order does not cover treatment, and the leak source is unknown. Stop, record the request, and refer to the responsible remediation manager for a revised scope and a competent assessment.

workedExamples.situation: A newly painted wall smells musty after rain, and the carpet next to it feels dry.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the correct next step?
workedExamples.reasoning: The moisture source has not been identified and may be somewhere other than the visible area. Record the observations, use a non-invasive questionnaire and photograph log, and refer the source to a qualified building investigation. Painting again would not correct the source.

workedExamples.situation: A manager asks for immediate demolition of a sealed cupboard that has recurring staining.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can a cleaner accept the instruction?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Demolition requires a revised scope, a competent assessment and specialist investigation. Stop, use the stop-work decision tree, and issue a controlled referral note.

workedExamples.situation: A ceiling collapses to reveal suspicious old insulation under sewage-affected plasterboard.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop work and isolate the area. Do not disturb the insulation. Treat the water as contaminated, escalate to a competent and, where required, licensed person, and document the isolation in the risk register.

workedExamples.situation: A worker brings a loose disposable mask and says it is enough for major demolition.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the worker ready to start?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Stop until a competent person has approved the PPE and the worker's readiness.

workedExamples.situation: A customer asks for a pathogen-free certificate after the cleaner has finished a visual clean.
workedExamples.reasoning: Only what was done and what was seen. A visual clean cannot establish a pathogen-free result. Record the unverified areas, state that independent clearance is required, and name the reviewer who must give it.

commonErrors.error: Treating a damp room as routine cleaning because the tenant asked for it.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the work order. Routine cleaning does not include remediation. Refer for a revised scope.

commonErrors.error: Painting or cleaning over a damp area and calling it fixed.
commonErrors.prevention: Identify and correct the moisture source first, then re-evaluate before any reoccupation decision.

commonErrors.error: Assuming the absence of visible growth means there is no hidden damage.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the warning signs and refer concealed damage for competent investigation.

commonErrors.error: Telling an occupant with respiratory symptoms that a room is safe.
commonErrors.prevention: Make no clearance or medical statement. Refer health questions to a clinician.

commonErrors.error: Disturbing old insulation or plasterboard under sewage-affected material without assessment.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, isolate, and escalate for asbestos and lead assessment by a competent and, where required, licensed person.

commonErrors.error: Wearing a loose disposable mask for a major demolition job.
commonErrors.prevention: Match PPE to the exposure, and verify the respirator program, training and fit before entry.

commonErrors.error: Using a domestic vacuum or aggressive dry brushing on a contaminated area.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the methods in the approved plan. These methods are unsuitable for contaminated areas.

commonErrors.error: Putting demolition debris into ordinary office bins.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse. Verify the authorised waste route before any handling.

commonErrors.error: Giving a customer a pathogen-free or clearance certificate after a visual clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Separate task completion, visual review and independent clearance. Name the reviewer who must clear the area.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This module does not grant authority to remediate, demolish, disturb building materials, handle contaminated water or waste, or certify any area as safe. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

Asbestos and lead disturbance, sewage remediation and certain waste handling are restricted to competent, and where the law requires, licensed people. In Victoria, friable asbestos removal needs a Class A licence, and non-friable asbestos can be removed under a Class B licence; the unlicensed allowance for non-friable asbestos covers an area of 10 square metres in total, and a total time of one hour in any period of seven days, which is cumulative across all employees (Asbestos Victoria, unlicensed asbestos removal page, which shows an 'Updated' label and no date), and friable asbestos has no such allowance. Work above these limits needs a licence, and this lesson does not grant one.

The sources are US EPA guidance for schools and commercial buildings. It is voluntary guidance, not Australian law, and the source states it requires local validation before learner use. The WA Health guideline (April 2024 version) is cited for Western Australia only. It sets no numerical health-based exposure limit for mould, and it describes a no-recurrence check at two to four weeks after remediation as an indicator of success rather than a formal clearance.
Reoccupation and verification decisions follow the applicable local and contractual requirements. They are separate from task completion.
Health questions go to a clinician. This module does not give medical advice or clearance.
No product, dilution, contact time, quantity or cleaning formula is given. Method selection follows the approved remediation plan.
Routine cleaning certificates do not establish remediation competence or the absence of mould, hidden damage or pathogens.

summary: Mould work is authorised by a plan and a competent supervisor. Routine cleaning is not remediation.
Find and correct the moisture source. Painting and wiping do not fix dampness.
No visible growth does not mean no hidden damage. Refer concealed damage.
Make no medical or clearance statements. Refer health questions to clinicians.
Flood, sewage, asbestos and lead need their own controls. Stop and escalate.
PPE and respirator readiness are verified before entry. Improvised protection is refused.
Containment and zoning are planned and approved before work starts.
Porous and uncertain materials need competent decisions, not a blanket treatment.
Use only the methods in the approved plan. Dry brushing and domestic vacuums are unsuitable.
Waste goes only by an authorised route. Separate task completion from independent clearance.

officialReferences.title: Guidelines for Managing Mould and Dampness-Related Public Health Risks in Buildings
officialReferences.covers: Western Australian guidance only. Check the current WA edition, and the state or territory health authority for other jurisdictions. Publisher: WA Department of Health.

officialReferences.title: Bushfire recovery: asbestos clean-up
officialReferences.covers: Victorian licence classes only (Class A for friable, Class B for non-friable asbestos). Check the licence rules for your state or territory. Publisher: WorkSafe Victoria.

officialReferences.title: Unlicensed asbestos removal
officialReferences.covers: Victorian unlicensed allowance for non-friable asbestos only: the area of asbestos-containing material to be removed does not exceed 10 square metres in total, and the total time asbestos removal work is performed in any period of seven days does not exceed one hour (this period is the cumulative total time the asbestos removal work is carried out by all employees over a period of seven days). Publisher: Asbestos Victoria (Victorian Government).

knowledgeChecks.question: A tenant asks a cleaner to treat a damp bedroom after a long leak, but the work order covers only routine cleaning. What should the cleaner do?
options: Treat the room, because the tenant has asked and the leak was clearly the landlord's fault
Stop and refer to the responsible remediation manager for a revised scope and competent assessment.
Treat the room lightly and note the leak on the job sheet, so the manager can see it later on

knowledgeChecks.question: A newly painted wall smells musty after rain. What is the correct next step?
options: Paint the wall again to cover the smell, since a fresh coat should hide the musty odour quickly
Assume the carpet is dry, so the wall is dry too, since the two are usually at the same level
Identify the moisture source through a non-invasive history, photograph log and building investigation referral.

knowledgeChecks.question: A manager asks for immediate demolition of a sealed cupboard with recurring staining. What is correct?
options: Stop, because demolition needs a revised scope, a competent assessment and specialist investigation.
Demolish it, because the manager has authority over the building and the cupboard is in the way
Open a small hole to look inside the cupboard, then decide what to do with the wall and the stains

knowledgeChecks.question: Old insulation is revealed under sewage-affected plasterboard after a ceiling collapse. What is the immediate response?
options: Remove the insulation quickly to make the area safe before the ceiling falls any further and the crew is put at risk
Stop work, isolate the area and escalate to a competent and, where required, licensed person, without disturbing the insulation.
Continue the clean with a mask and gloves, since the insulation is only a small part of the area and the room is wet

knowledgeChecks.question: An occupant with respiratory symptoms asks whether the room is now safe. What is the response?
options: Confirm the room is safe, because the clean is finished and the area looks dry to the eye now
Tell the occupant the room is safe for children only, since adults are at more risk here
Make no clearance statement. Record the scope and refer the health question to a clinician.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker brings a loose disposable mask and says it is adequate for major demolition. What is correct?
options: Stop until a competent person has matched the PPE to the exposure and verified the worker's training and fit.
Accept it, because the worker is confident and has used a mask like it on many other jobs before
Accept it if the job is only a few hours long and the room is well ventilated during the work

knowledgeChecks.question: Cleaning activity may carry airborne particles into an occupied corridor. What must happen first?
options: Clean the corridor quickly while the occupants are out, so the job is finished before they return
Plan an approved zoning and communication plan so that occupants and clean areas are protected.
Leave the door open so that the air moves out of the room and the corridor stays fresh and clear

knowledgeChecks.question: Saturated drywall and timber sit beside washable metal fixtures. How should the material be treated?
options: Clean all of it with the same method, since the metal and the drywall can be treated in the same way
Dry the drywall quickly with a heater and keep it, since it will recover once the moisture is gone
Classify each material by uncertainty and likely referral, and refer porous items for competent project decisions.

knowledgeChecks.question: A domestic vacuum and aggressive dry brushing are proposed for a contaminated area. What is correct?
options: Reject them as unsuitable, and compare the methods against the approved remediation plan.
Use them, because they are quick, cheap, and easy to set up at the site on the day
Use them only if the area is small and the contamination is limited to one spot

knowledgeChecks.question: A contractor suggests putting demolition debris into ordinary office waste bins. What is correct?
options: Agree, because office bins are emptied every day and the debris will be gone by the morning
Refuse, and verify the disposal, transport and contractor authorisations before any handling.
Agree if the debris is in sealed bags and the bins are kept shut until the collection

knowledgeChecks.question: A landlord wants new paint before a leak is repaired. What should be explained?
options: Painting first is fine, because the leak can be fixed later once the paint is dry and the room is occupied
Painting is only needed if the wall is visibly stained, so the landlord can wait on the leak repair for now
Painting over affected surfaces does not remedy dampness, so the leak repair and moisture re-evaluation must come first.

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer asks for a pathogen-free certificate after a visual clean. What can be written?
options: Only what was done and what was seen, with the unverified areas named and the independent reviewer requirement stated.
A pathogen-free certificate, because the area looks clean and the crew has finished every visible task
A statement that the room is safe to occupy with no further checks, since the visual clean was thorough
